And then when we got into quarantine, I started eating more for breakfast and a bigger meal in the evening. So I think I probably was three or four pounds heavy going into the flight. So I think the weight loss may be overplayed a little bit, because I think I— —had a few extra pounds, and then plus I don't think that maybe I picked the right weight up on the rolling scales. But that's neither here nor there, you know.

the interviewers: Well, we can probably show you something about that when we get your lab material pulled together. I think we'd be able to give you a better handle on that— as to whether it really was something that had to do with the zero-G state or not. We hope we'll be able to do that.

title: NASA-UAP-D026, Apollo 14 Debriefing, 1971
text:
the crew: If I could just add a general comment, which I think reflects the consensus here of the three of us: With respect to the food in general— the type of food, the method by which it was packaged, and the degree to which we liked or disliked it— it was primarily a function of the level of activity in the flight plan. The business of going into the pantry and taking time to select foods and drinks and so on is fine during the quiet periods of coast. But things like spoon packages are good only if the level of activity is not too high; certainly if the level of activity is high, the wet packs and the cans are about all you want to take time to fool with. I think this is a general comment that really reflects our consensus. It was a time-consuming part of the day to prepare meals— get them out of the food box, get them all laid out, cut all the tops off of them, get all the water into them, get them massaged, and go about eating. Get the pill back in there when you throw it back. It took a lot of time; it's an effort. And it's a lot easier to open up a can and a wet pack— then you think it's a lot of trouble to mix it up with juice— but that way you've got your meal and you're through and you're on your way.

the interviewers: Okay— the cooking problem, quote, is still a problem, which has been fairly common, I guess.

the crew: Yeah, I think if you've got plenty of time, you don't mind spending an hour or so. As a matter of fact, it's a very pleasant hour— it gets rid of that tiredness very effectively. But I would say, in my case, watching these guys eat, they went right down the menu. And so I thought, I really should do that, but I just didn't have an inclination to eat that much. Even though you know in your own mind, hey, you ought to do this, you ought to keep yourself eating just as much as you possibly can— I just couldn't get around to doing it. In fact, several times I'd mix the food up, and then by the time I'd eaten a couple of packages, I just couldn't get to the third package, so I'd put it back in the pantry.

the interviewers: Well, Stu, one of the things that's going to come out of that is— somebody reading the debriefing itself, the obvious question comes up: was your lack of appetite just plain lack of appetite, or did you— —as far as the gut was concerned at all? Anything that you felt was pathological in your loss of appetite, due to the environment or anything?

the crew: No, no, I don't think there's anything of that. Like I say, I think it boils down to just too much food. If you bundle up one of those meals, there's just too much there to eat.

the interviewers: Were any of you ever thirsty in flight? Did you feel thirst?

the crew: Yeah, you were dry quite a bit. You'd have the sensation of dryness, and water or juice would take care of it once in a while. Yeah.

the interviewers: While we're at it, we might just wipe out the water thing— did you guys drink the water in your suits? On EVA?

title: NASA-UAP-D026, Apollo 14 Debriefing, 1971
text:
the crew: I did— I didn't drink all of it, I just drank about a third of it. One drank all of his; I drank about a third of mine, I guess. On the first one, I don't know how much of mine I drank— I thought I emptied the bag, but apparently the walls of the bag got around the drink tube and I didn't get it all out, because it drained down around my neck during the sleep period. I had a leaky one also, which I took out between EVAs.

the interviewers: Did you fill them up again when you went out on the second EVA?

the crew: No.

the interviewers: And you drank about— you think you drank about a third of yours both times?

the crew: Yeah, I didn't really stop to drink too much. And I drank all mine the second EVA— I can't remember whether I drank it all or not. If I didn't, there may be some still in it. Hey, why don't I comment, while we're on that eating, before I forget— we ran completely out of these bite-sized packages. To me, that was the best thing we had: these little turkey sandwiches, cheese sandwiches, and that sort of thing, because that was a no-sweat operation. You just clip that off, and a can of juice, and you could go at it. So I really liked those, and I ate all those I could get my hands on. We ran out of those— well, we ran out of most everything else. Not really— I had all kinds of food. If I may make a comment, if Stu doesn't mind, about his eating and drinking habits. This flight plan is really something that he worked on and developed for the flight. It's a busy flight plan— a full one. And it was my impression that he was more interested in being sure the flight plan was done properly than in eating. Oh yeah, I think that affected it to a great degree— which again gets back to the level of activity. If you guys can get, for example, in those drink bags, a little diaphragm on the end that you stick over a needle— pump the water in that way, shake it up, pull the plug out, and drink it out of the same deal— that would be a lot easier for those drinks.

the interviewers: For the juices and things, you mean?

the crew: Yeah— all the cutting. So you don't end up having to feel you've got to drink the whole damn thing once you get it done.

title: NASA-UAP-D026, Apollo 14 Debriefing, 1971
text:
the crew: You see, you've got a drink bag and a little gnarled thing that's all sucked in— the plastic is all folded down. Unless you cut it exactly right, first of all you can't get it in the nozzle without having it leak. Then you get it all done, and then you've got to go cut the other end. And I was just thinking maybe there might be an easier way— put a diaphragm fitting on there that you could stick over a hypodermic type of thing and get the water in that way. Might be a little quicker. Anything you do to make it easier is going to help increase the consumption, particularly during busy time periods.

the interviewers: Okay. Could we get you— now this is going to involve really just Al and Ed. We'd like you to describe, as well as you can, the things you did with your bioinstrumentation harnesses, because it's very hard for us to be sure exactly what happened. We don't have that stuff back yet— we've got to develop a plan to troubleshoot it. And as I understand, the thing that happened with yours, Al, just from our point of view—

the crew: You want the actions, not the words, huh?

the interviewers: Pardon?

the crew: You want the actions, not the words.

the interviewers: The actions, not the words, yeah. Okay— well, you can say some of the words too. From our point of view, what happened with your particular harness is: everything was fine when everybody left the MSOB. When you got into the spacecraft— right after, apparently when you were getting cinched down somehow— we had about three minutes or so of good data on you after you were in the couch. Then we began to get erratic data. It began to wander— the baseline began to wander all over the place. That continued to get worse and worse, and pretty soon it was going— —just full scale, which was totally unreadable. So the question was— it was a question about hatch closure at that point in time. We decided right then— I said, well, hell, we're going to go without that, because I'm sure it's a sensor and that's the only way to get at it anyway. We asked you then to try and press on those things. And we went back to the MSOB from the firing room to catch that pass, and there you were— whap— it was beautiful, just as if nothing had ever happened. And you hadn't done a damn thing, because then we asked, have you done anything? Now, as we understand, when you looked at that sensor you did have some material that had leaked out from underneath it, and you— And we understand that you cleaned up and replaced that sensor. Is that right?

the crew: We didn't replace the sensor, no.

title: NASA-UAP-D026, Apollo 14 Debriefing, 1971
text:
the crew: Cleaned it off, refilled it, put a new sticky-back on it, and put it back on.

the interviewers: Yeah, okay. That was the first time— we asked you to do that then because we thought we'd get it out of the way before you got into it. Now then, you had another—

the crew: The CWG adapter— that one time in the flight they said my comm was terrible, right? We had a spare adapter, so we changed that. Exactly when that was, I don't know— that was pretty early too. I think it was the first day.

the interviewers: Yeah, your comm was terrible, right. Al, that didn't have anything to do with the launch problem, because—

the crew: No.

the interviewers: And we had respiration on you— you could see respiration, but we didn't have the ECG.

the crew: That was very reassuring to me.

the interviewers: How can you correlate the reappearance of your EKG signal with any flight-plan activity you might have been doing?

the crew: I sure can't— I'm just as mystified about that as you are. I tried to press through the suit and everything; you can't feel anything through the suit.

the interviewers: Well, you were free then though— you had your helmet and gloves off. It was one hour and thirty minutes GET. I don't know if that rings any bells to you.

the crew: Helmets and gloves are off at that time. We're moving around with the post-insertion checklist, and there's some movement in the couch— I dive in and get some things and pull them out, that sort of stuff.

the interviewers: It probably just got to be— it was in the cinching-down in the couch that it probably loosened that edge of that sensor somehow a little bit. I don't know why, but—

title: NASA-UAP-D026, Apollo 14 Debriefing, 1971
text:
the crew: —or put a crimp in a lead, or brought it into contact with something else. Yeah, because it sure came back fine after that.

the interviewers: Okay, then the second time— what else did you have with yours, Al? What else did you do?

the crew: The only other thing I noticed was, about the next-to-last day, that the thread coupling between the sensor harness and the belt— the little jack and bushing on top of the signal conditioner— it stripped the threads. I could get it to hold a little bit, and apparently the signal was fine, then it would slip off.

the interviewers: It came back beautifully when you tightened it.

the crew: But then when I unsuited at the end, I noticed that was loose. So the threads apparently stripped on that— apparently I got it cranked down too hard.

the interviewers: Did you routinely disconnect that connector at the signal conditioner for sleep, or for bowel movements, or anything like that?

the crew: For bowel movements and swabbing down— the cleaning-out process. Anytime you pulled your clothes off— to either change clothes, or put on the LCG, or use the blue bags, whatever— we all undid those.

the interviewers: Okay. And then you didn't replace anything— you didn't have to reseat any sensor after that? That was the only other thing you had, the signal cable.

the crew: That was the only time I took a sensor off— that first time. And that call was correct, because when we took it off we could see the seepage of the electrolyte.

the interviewers: Right, good. Okay— how about yours then, Ed?

the crew: The only thing I replaced was that one sensor.

title: NASA-UAP-D026, Apollo 14 Debriefing, 1971
text:
the interviewers: Which one was that?

the crew: And it was the same one.

the interviewers: The whole sensor?

the crew: I don't mean replace— we pulled it off, cleaned it out, refilled it with electrolyte, put it back on. It was the same sensor.

the interviewers: You did not take the harness out of the kit and replace the whole thing?

the crew: No.

the interviewers: Okay— because we thought you had done that. Well, you called and asked for that, but there wasn't time to do it, so we took— I'm glad you couldn't hear what we said when you guys said that— we took the chance that the real problem was simply the sensor and the electrolyte.

the crew: And that's what it was. That's exactly what it was. We couldn't have picked a worse time, from the standpoint of timeline. We were just getting ready to go into the lab— everybody's all asses and elbows and suits and underwear and gear and books, everything all over the place. And I was sitting here half-dressed. I didn't want to go any further until we got a go on it.

the interviewers: We couldn't get the high bit-rate up for you guys to look at it. And so there just wasn't any time left.

the crew: So we changed that one and I went ahead and dressed.

the interviewers: Hey, Ed— when you came up there, you gave us about two minutes when the high-gain did lock on, and we got two minutes of data, and it still showed— —the loose sensor. Now, what did you do the second time? You came up, asked us how the data looked, and we said it looked poor yet, and we gave you a no-go on the suiting to change out the harness. Recall exactly the sequence of events.

title: NASA-UAP-D026, Apollo 14 Debriefing, 1971
text:
the crew: When I called and asked you to check it, as far as I know we did nothing after that except make sure everything was cinched down, and went ahead and dressed.

the interviewers: Didn't you do something with the fluid in there?

the crew: Yeah, but I had already done it at that point. I changed the electrolyte when I called and asked you guys to check it.

the interviewers: You see, the first time you called it in, it was poor, and that was the basis for the call to change out the whole harness— we said, well, it wasn't that sensor, and we didn't have time to talk to you because LOS was coming up. So we said, go ahead and change out the whole thing. But whatever you did subsequently corrected it, because it came back beautifully. So we assumed you had just changed out the whole thing.

the crew: Siggy [sic], now that you mention it— I just can't remember precisely when we changed it, but I'm thinking it was already changed at that point.

the interviewers: Oh, okay. And Ed, was this the lower sternal sensor— same as Al's?

the crew: It was the lower sternal. Remember, they changed it— it was the electrolyte that was replaced. Yes.

the interviewers: What I mean is, taking it off and cleaning it and putting the new one back— just sticking it back. Okay. And you think he did that before LOS? Yeah, he probably did. What we're thinking happened now is it probably took a while for it to seat properly, and when he came around it was good again— because his stayed good then. And then we were having trouble with yours going in. You began to get this wandering baseline on yours again— after we got into the LM [sic]. So there was a question in our minds— is there any way we could get that better? We were trying to figure some way. Could you reach around when you were in the suit? Is there any way you could get at that thing— if, after the EVA, you ended up taking the helmet off, could you get down into the suit through the neck ring?

the crew: You really have to have the upper torso garment— the upper part of the torso garment— clear of the body in order to be able to feel that. There's no way you can definitely tell, even if the other guy goes through the back zipper and around in front. We tried that on the ground.

title: NASA-UAP-D026, Apollo 14 Debriefing, 1971
text:
the interviewers: Really?

the crew: That's pretty hard to do. The most you can do is press on it. After all that time quarantining, that's pretty dangerous too. Yeah— depends on where his hands end up.

the interviewers: Okay, all right.

the crew: Forget the EVAs— just keep fooling with my sensors. You've got two hours to do that.

the interviewers: We've got two hours. Okay. Did— the thing we got from the sleep, which I think is fairly well covered; if you have anything to add to that, we'd like you to. But what we got out of it is that all of you pretty well never really had a solid, long sleep period— that it was broken, things like a couple of hours at a time. And I gather the reasons for that varied. You had some difficulty with wanting to feel some pressure— in Ed's case I know, and Al mentioned this too. And Stu didn't like the couch. And then you ended up in the LM, where it was being in the suits all the time, and the tilt of the LM too. Both those things probably had a lot to do with the sleep activity. Is there anything else you think you can add? Did you feel that you were rested enough to do the task, even with the sleep that you had?

the crew: Yeah, but I think we were working on reserves. I did too. Well, there were 2 days that we felt sloppy. One was the second day out, after the excitement of the launch and all that activity, and becoming acclimated to the new environment. We felt like we weren't really clicking along too well on the second day out. And then the day after TDI— although we all apparently slept better after TDI that night. We were getting things done, but the little things weren't being handled as neatly as we would like. So these are the only 2 days we felt we weren't on top of the flight plan. I think, Chuck, for no longer than we worked— for 9 days— you can get along on a fairly small amount of sleep; your reserves and your discipline and everything else make you do the job properly. But in my case, I felt very strongly— —that I was on reserves, that physically I was going downhill.

title: NASA-UAP-D026, Apollo 14 Debriefing, 1971
text:
the crew: It was of some concern to me that I wasn't getting enough sleep. I knew I wasn't getting enough sleep, and yet I felt fairly wide awake and alert on most of the days, except the 2 days I was talking about.

the interviewers: How do you mean insecure— because of this wanting something?

the crew: Yeah— wanting to feel like you were in a bed, the best I can say. Wanting to feel some pressure, to be lying on something. It was pleasant.

the interviewers: Turn the tape recorder on. I knew we'd get back to that.

the crew: It was really a pleasant experience to be in zero-G during the daytime, I thought. It wasn't quite so pleasant an experience at night.

the interviewers: Well, did you feel— that brings up this thing— I gather from Al's comments in particular, this business of using your legs and your feet to try and hang on to something, which has been described by other guys too at some length. Did you have a feeling that that was the cause of this muscle business in your back? Because that's been described, and they've never been able to really put a handle on why they felt they had it. They had this sort of feeling that if they could just stretch that real good, it would be great. Do you think it's due to the fact that you were trying to lock onto something?

the crew: Yeah, that's what I analyzed after the first couple days. We discussed it, as a matter of fact. So we started exercising, and then deliberately took time out to relax— not only during the sleep period, but also trying to adapt ourselves to a relaxed state during the awake periods, in the seats or on the optics or in the tunnel. And after the second day, it kind of went away— that small-of-the-back problem was gone after a couple of days. In fact, I was kind of surprised at that. I woke up that first morning— my back had bothered me during the night— and I didn't realize that Ed's back was bothering him at that time too. I said, I really didn't get that much sleep, but this sounds crazy as all hell, because I can lay on that big fine king-size bed at the house, and if I lay there for say 10 or 11 hours, the small of my back bothers me. And I said to these guys, hey, this is crazy: I didn't sleep that much last night, but my back feels just like I got about 11 hours of sleep. And they said, well, mine does too. Then we got to talking about it. But it was there, and it was very conscious to me that first night. In fact, I thought probably my back kept me from going to sleep as much as the new environment did, rather than the zero-G, because I was always conscious of my back bothering me.

the interviewers: Did you ever think about taking aspirin or anything for that? Did you ever have that in mind?

the crew: I didn't take aspirin at all.

the interviewers: For the ache?

title: NASA-UAP-D026, Apollo 14 Debriefing, 1971
text:
the crew: I think, until the time we discussed it, I was convinced that the reason I was feeling bad in the back was just not urinating for so damn long during that hold on the first day. I did think that. And then after we started discussing it, I said, well, that may not be the problem— or if so, that's just part of the problem. Everybody's got it. And I agree with Al that it has something to do with the way you try to use your feet to stabilize yourself.

the interviewers: I wondered if you wouldn't think that.

the crew: And I found— I believe, although I couldn't see myself— that when I was relaxing in the spacecraft in zero-G, I was in a curved position, and it felt good to throw the shoulders back and straighten out, or to take the Exergym and get some tension on those back muscles. You tend to assume sort of a fetal position— if you totally relax, your legs float up into a semi-seat, your hands float out about like this, and your back bends some. It assumes that kind of position if you let all your muscles go. One of the good things for that back is just exactly that position. And I know that first night when my back was bothering me, I'd reach down and grab hold of my booties and lay there pulling some pressure on my legs, and it would really help the small of the back. I found both things worked— either straighten out to put some tension on the back muscles, or, as Stu says, double on up and pull the other way.

the interviewers: How about when you got back onto the carrier and got into a bed for the first time in a 1G environment? Did you have any feeling that you were real heavy, that you were sinking into the bed? Did you have that when you were on a table— on the x-ray table or anything of that sort?

the crew: No, not really.

the interviewers: None of you experienced that. How about the weight of clothes? Did you have a feeling that your pants were too heavy, or that they were falling or anything like that when you first got back?

the crew: You're on your back. And I remember thinking of that— the first thing, when I laid down in the bunk, I stretched out on my back and thought, gee, I've been this way for 9 days, I think I'll turn over. So I rolled over on my stomach. It felt pretty good.

the interviewers: Did any of you have any dreams at all? Did you ever dream of flying at all?

the crew: I did, but I couldn't for the life of me recall them.

the interviewers: Well, that doesn't matter.

the crew: Yeah, I had dreams.

title: NASA-UAP-D026, Apollo 14 Debriefing, 1971
text:
the interviewers: But you did have dream activity, at least in the zero-G state. Good.

the crew: Yeah, I think of that heavy feeling, Chuck. The only time I noticed it was after we landed— we were still in the spacecraft, we unstrapped, and it was bobbing around a little bit, but not too much. I got down on the lower equipment bay right away. In the first couple of steps, it was a combination of the rocking of the spacecraft and being in 1G again, for perhaps 30 seconds, no more than that. I started doing some deep knee bends right away, maybe 10 or 12 of those, and I was right back home again and continued to feel that way. No muscle soreness, no feeling of heaviness or anything from there on out.

the interviewers: This feeling you experienced when you first went down in the lower equipment bay— was that all over, or was it just heaviness in the legs? Did you feel heavy all over for a few seconds?

the crew: Just felt heavy all over. I think it was all over.

the interviewers: How about when you first got some G on reentry? Did you have a sensation that you had a lot more G than you were really registering?

the crew: I did.— I don't remember anything over 2G. Was I supposed to? Of course— these 2 guys were... you know that.

the interviewers: You don't, huh? You blanked out, huh?

the crew: No, I think you become very sensitive to G. Even ullage in the spacecraft— that'd be about the only time you'd really feel a G, the ullage, as well as the SPS engine, of course. But on entry, certainly, as you're going through 1G, it certainly doesn't seem like 1G. You're sensitive to the G. I wasn't quite as busy during that initial period as they were— I didn't have tracking tasks to keep me occupied, so I probably felt it more, or was conscious of it more than they did. And it felt to me like one hell of a load. In particular, my one task was to watch the time, and I couldn't get my arm up to see the watch until after peak G let off. At about 4 or 5 G, I could pull my arm up and take a look at it. And I had the same sensation Al did— right after I got out of the couch, I felt very, very heavy, and then with just a little bit of motion it seemed to go away. I'd say the return to normal described a very sharp rise and then an asymptote to 1G, because I still stumbled a couple of times getting out of the helicopter. But I felt fine, except I just didn't have the sureness of footing I would have liked.

the interviewers: That didn't last long as far as footing. That's an interesting thing— the Russians had some real marked mobility problems after their 18-day flight that lasted for days. You didn't have anything of that degree; we've never had anything like that. We've always had some initial footing problem, just getting used to being back in a 1G environment, and you're on a ship too, which is moving around. But this didn't last for any of you longer than a few minutes, really, getting out of the helicopter. How about putting your feet in the right place— did you feel like you were walking normally?

title: NASA-UAP-D026, Apollo 14 Debriefing, 1971
text:
the crew: No, I think up to the point we got in the MQF, it took a little care to make sure my foot was going where it was supposed to go, but it wasn't out of the ordinary. It wasn't out of the ordinary— really severe or anything. It seemed to be improving very rapidly: from a very heavy state for the first 30 to 45 seconds after I got out of the couch, to within an hour or so after I was in the MQF, when the footing was very sure. But I do remember stumbling once going into the MQF from the helicopter, and I didn't see anything to stumble over— I just stumbled. Then again, you'd do that right now: if you're going to walk out that door with a television camera on you and walk up the steps, you'd be more conscious of your footing whether or not you'd been in zero-G. You've just come back from a flight and people are going to be watching how you're walking, so it's in your mind— you've got to walk this 30 feet to the MQF, and naturally you're more conscious of where you're going to put your foot. I may have psyched myself into stumbling for that reason, but nevertheless I did stumble— in spite of the fact that I was conscious that the TV cameras were on.

the interviewers: Did you notice any distortion of your facial features at all? When you look at the in-flight TV, as we watched you inside the spacecraft, you get the impression that your faces are not like they are now— that they're much rounder. Is that true? Did you feel that when you were looking at each other?

the crew: No, but I observed it when I saw a picture of us taken from that TV, and I didn't think anything about it until you mentioned it. You look quite round— much different than you do now.

the interviewers: But you weren't aware of it looking at each other?

the crew: You know, Al Bean made a comment about that in the 12 report— that after they got in orbit, he looked around and everybody looked 20 pounds heavier. I remembered that, and I looked at these guys, and they looked just as bad then as they do now.

the interviewers: The 12 crew, I guess, were the ones most impressed with that of anybody. They even felt they had redness of the face for several hours after they first achieved orbit.

the crew: Well, the general feeling of fullness is there, I think. But just to look at a person and see his face puffed up— I didn't notice that at all. Maybe it was just lack of observation.

the interviewers: I heard that for the first 5 hours it was really good that way [sic]. Did you have any sensation that, in the first 24 hours in flight, you urinated more than you normally would— more than you did the rest of the flight time?

title: NASA-UAP-D026, Apollo 14 Debriefing, 1971
text:
the crew: I don't know— that's a hard thing to remember.

the interviewers: Do you have any idea that you did that at all?

the crew: I wouldn't say that at all. I never used my UCTA. That first one was a whopper, I know that.

the interviewers: Of course, you had a lot of excitement to make it a whopper anyway, so it's hard to tell.

the crew: No real feeling one way or the other on that.

the interviewers: Can you comment on the work you did on EVA out on the lunar surface, as far as what you felt versus your ground training? Did you think it was harder, easier, or about the same? And secondly— did either of you feel really physically tired, to the point that you knew you were really tired during the EVAs, even going up Cone?

the crew: I felt, of course, it was an order of magnitude easier than 1G training— just no comparison at all, as we expected it to be. As far as being tired— I'd already made up my mind that I did not want to sweat on the moon, that I was going to keep the water up and keep resting enough. So I never really felt tired. I did feel occasionally that I was approaching the point where I'd have to have more cooling or take a break, but it wasn't because of a tired feeling— it was the desire to program and plan consumables the way we wanted to, and not be hot. So I felt in my mind that I was stopping short of the point of fatigue, as a deliberate plan of not wanting to use up consumables.

the interviewers: How about you, Al?

the crew: Well, it's kind of hard to equate the preflight stuff with the flight stuff. In the first place, you're not using the LCG in the preflight stuff, and you're lifting essentially 1G pieces of equipment around and so on. So it's pretty hard to equate the two in my mind, as to whether it was harder or easier in flight from the standpoint of total work output. But certainly, from the standpoint of ease of mobility, as Ed says, it's a lot easier to get around— you travel a lot faster and easier on the lunar surface, as a general comment to start with. On EVA-1, I did not feel uncomfortable at any time at all. On EVA-2, the fact that I was aware of the workload was manifested primarily in the respiration rate, as opposed to anything else. I didn't feel as though the deep body heat was going up too much— I think primarily because of the circulating fluid in the LCG. I was not aware of any profuse sweating, just a little faint tinge of sweating, a blush, when I went to medium flow on the water. And of course you're not really aware of an increase in heart rate either, unless you specifically stop and measure it somehow. So to me the thing most obvious about the increased workload was the respiration rate. At times, climbing the steepest grade of Cone Crater, we stopped and decompressed. But from the standpoint of being tired to the degree where we didn't want to press on after a short rest period— no, I didn't feel that at any time, until after the 2 days were over and we were back in the command module. I never really felt like I was behind the curve as far as the total workload was concerned.

the interviewers: Well, we'll try and give you some firm feeling for what happened with your EVAs when we do this later. We can show you actually what went on— you did have some times where you both got heart rates up in the 150 area. And this is why we felt the way we did. Your respiratory rates were very audible, and we didn't have a respiration trace on you at that time, as you know. But you did have very audible respiratory rates, and it was obvious that you were increasing those. And Al, I think you kept yours on min for a long time, and then when you did turn up to medium flow, you left it there only a short period, and it didn't kick your rate down as much, because you were still maintaining some of that heat in there. It wasn't enough to make you sweat, apparently. And then when you started turning it on a little bit longer each time, it just settled right back down— you didn't have any trouble with it at all after that. But both of you came down very well: when you'd rest, your rates dropped down. That's contrary to what happened on 12, where they didn't drop down when they rested. Yours came right on down as soon as you stopped the activity.

title: NASA-UAP-D026, Apollo 14 Debriefing, 1971
text:
the interviewers: Do you have any recommendations about extending EVAs now? Do you feel it would be possible, with proper consumables— that it's physically possible to do that?

the crew: I sure do. The thing that bothered me was worrying about consumables, and knowing that we were getting a higher metabolic load— a higher heart rate, more oxygen consumption going up Cone Crater— and that I was spending more time between minimum and intermediate cooling, because we were deliberately rushing to make up time. I started worrying about consumables, especially the water and the oxygen. I felt that was the limiting factor— I didn't feel that I was the limiting factor; just the oxygen and water I was consuming were bothering me.

the interviewers: Well, we tried to give you the word. We thought you were trying to save consumables.

the crew: Yeah, we were.

the interviewers: Yeah, and understandably so. And so we wanted you to know that you had enough— that you could go to medium flow without really getting yourself in a hole. That was the thing we wanted you to know.

the crew: After you did that, I spent considerably more time between minimum and intermediate.

the interviewers: Yeah, you did. You both did then.

the crew: Incidentally, on the comment about total workload with respect to the 2-day period— I wouldn't want to see a crew ever plan to do any more than we did in those 2 days. As far as I'm concerned, that's about as heavy a workload as anybody ought to do. And certainly if you're going to go out for longer periods of EVA, you ought to allow longer periods of rest— and make sure somehow that they get the rest. Just allowing the time doesn't necessarily assure rest.

the interviewers: I agree with that. Well, tell me— if you had, in the LEM— I gather one of the things you think would help, of course, would be getting out of the suit. That certainly would help; you could get out of a suit on the moon, no question about that. And if you had something for sleep, would you take it? Would you guys have taken it in the LEM if you'd had something for sleep, do you think?

the crew: I don't think so. I don't know about Ed, but I certainly don't take that kind of medication here on the ground. It's an individual thing, quite obviously— it just depends. You try to do things in space as closely as you can to the ground environment; that's probably the way everybody would do it. So if you have people who do that on the ground, it probably would help them. I'd prefer to see us use a more natural means of getting to sleep, as opposed to an artificial one.

the interviewers: You'd like to have something to sleep on— is that what you're saying? Back to that again.

title: NASA-UAP-D026, Apollo 14 Debriefing, 1971
text:
the crew: I think the suit's the big thing, as far as I was concerned.

the interviewers: Yeah, it keeps coming up.

the crew: You couldn't roll around. You couldn't roll around in a hammock, and the damn neck ring was hitting the back of the neck. There was one thing, Chuck, about fatigue: the only muscle I felt fatigued was the hand muscle in the right hand, because of the glove.

the interviewers: Because you were fighting that glove.

the crew: Yeah. And working the core tubes — unscrewing the core tubes, one of them I couldn't get by myself, and getting the caps off of them. That was very fatiguing, and that arm gave out.

the interviewers: How about when you were carrying the barbell out there? You said you had to do it like this.

the crew: That was tiring, but just because it's so cumbersome and it was flopping all around. But I eventually put it across my arms like that, and aside from the workload of carrying it out, it was no problem.

the interviewers: Was the weight different, seemed different? Because you commented at the time, and it looked like you were having trouble getting out there with that thing. Was it the weight of it, or just the fact that it was vibrating — that it was sort of like a fishing rod?

the crew: Mostly the vibration of it, just the flopping of it. However, I think it was heavier than I expected from the one-sixth-G mockup. But we had never carried it that far in training, and I think we've made that recommendation — that at least once the guys ought to carry it the whole way. It was primarily the flopping of those weights on the end that was giving me trouble.

the interviewers: Okay, let's get to this bowel movement thing and the crimps and so forth. You had a good comment in there that that went fairly well — you all did the same thing we do preflight anyway. Now, how did it work out? Do you remember? Can you tell us each one how you went? I gather Ed went almost to the end without having one, according to a comment. Where did you go? When did you—

the crew: I went to the morning of the 8th day — that was the first one. And that's the only one I was in. I didn't plan it that way.

title: NASA-UAP-D026, Apollo 14 Debriefing, 1971
text:
the interviewers: And that's the only one you had planned?

the crew: What I wanted to do was have one bowel movement before we went to the surface, so that would take care of that period of time. I went around with a bag on my fanny for about 12 hours hoping I could do something, and never did. At one point I even wished we had a laxative aboard to help me do that — I'm not sure that's a good idea, but it sure seemed like it at the time. I was really concerned that I'd need to have a bowel movement while we were on the surface. But I got through that period and figured, well, we've got it made; it'll be good to get back to the command module and use the bag. And I still couldn't — it wasn't until the 8th day, and that was a whopper.

the interviewers: Did you ever get any cramps or anything with it? You never had any gut disturbance at all?

the crew: No cramps, nothing. I wasn't uncomfortable — I didn't even have a feeling of fullness.

the interviewers: How about you? How did your cycle go?

the crew: Well, I had one and a half bags on the 3rd day, I believe it was, and then another bag on about the 7th day.

the interviewers: And no problem? Normal consistency and so forth, as far as you could tell?

the crew: No problems — normal consistency and function. But that's really uncivilized; we've got to find a better method.

the interviewers: I agree with you.

the crew: The total hygiene thing in this is so archaic, it's unbelievable. We just have to do better than that if we're going to keep people in space. It's really the only time it didn't feel civilized — that whole process, the whole mess, and the ability to clean up afterwards. The ability to maintain personal hygiene throughout the flight is archaic; we need better equipment.

the interviewers: Yeah, the whole mess. That's a big mess. How about you?

title: NASA-UAP-D026, Apollo 14 Debriefing, 1971
text:
the crew: I went to 80 hours — that was the first one. I remember distinctly, because between 80 and 81 hours, approaching LOI, I said, well, I'm going to do it. Preflight I anticipated I might have to use the bag more than that, because in my normal course of events it's very common for me to hit the head at least twice a day. So I was pleasantly surprised that I got to 80 hours. And then I had one other one — it was after TEI, I guess the next day after TEI. I don't remember the GET or the time frame. I can't even associate it with anything except these guys in their gas masks. I don't know what else was going on at that time.

the interviewers: When did you first start to use the nose drops? How far into the flight — do you remember what day?

the crew: Third day, wasn't it? Third, I think. Third day.

the interviewers: I'm a little bit confused about your description. You're describing this fullness — was that due to the weightlessness, or do you think it was an oxygen effect, just due to the drying and so forth?

the crew: I never felt that dry. At the time I thought it could have been either or both, so I just treated it symptomatically with about one drop in each nostril, and it was completely effective for the next 10 to 12 hours.

the interviewers: You could hear it — this is fairly routine. You hear it in the guys' voices; you know they're doing it. You hear this full feeling that they have. Sometimes they get a little hoarse sensation with it too. You described it very well yesterday — sometimes in the mornings you'd wake up and be better.

the crew: I don't know, that's kind of a subjective feeling. I kind of felt that maybe the whole full-head sensation was related to a readjustment of the whole cardiovascular system, and therefore if you could relax a little bit in the evening, it ought to help it. That's my theory — maybe I kind of wished it that way. It's just a general feeling, nothing to substantiate quantitatively. As far as the nose drops are concerned, they helped with the mucus, but didn't help the overall fullness sensation.

the interviewers: Did they work all right? I know we've got a special case here, but did they work all right?

the crew: Just like they should have. It cleared out the mucus temporarily, for a few hours.

title: NASA-UAP-D026, Apollo 14 Debriefing, 1971
text:
the interviewers: And you — what about now? Did you just give yourself too big a slug? Is that what happened?

the crew: I think I probably did, Chuck — I'm sure that's what happened. I hadn't used any up to that point, but on entry I thought, well, I'll just use some of these beauties. And I think I gave myself too big a dose in the right nostril, because my eyes started watering and I could feel it in my sinuses and everything else. But it lasted maybe an hour. I did that a couple, three hours prior to entry, and an hour later most of the symptoms had gone away — either that, or you get close to entry and stop worrying about it. But I overdid it. I hardly ever take any nose drops, so maybe I got too much in there. It's probably pretty powerful stuff. It is powerful. I know that in 1G here, if I take more than a couple of drops of Afrin — if I use drops instead of spray — I get the same effect. It's a burning and a real drying sensation. And it wasn't a lack of briefing or not trying it before flight; I think I was just a little overzealous in the application. You know, two drops are good, give it four.

the interviewers: Did you get a tachycardia with that? Did you get a real increase in heart rate?

the crew: Oh, I don't have the foggiest idea.

the interviewers: You didn't feel it anyway? It pumped a little more adrenaline. He got mad at us for suggesting that we use the goddamn thing.

the crew: Yeah, I was ticked off at the suggestion.

the interviewers: Did you all have some evidence in your ears? On the first exam, when Bill saw you, you were having some bubbles in there. Did you have any sensation during reentry that you were having trouble clearing your ears, any of you?

the crew: No sensations at all. That was surprising to me — I was looking for it. I had no problem at all, not a bit. I could feel the pressure change. I think maybe it's because the atmosphere is dry, but if you were doing a lot of talking, I'd notice myself sounding full and I'd say, gee, I'm sounding like that — and my head wasn't constantly full at all, but I could tell in my voice that I was sounding that way.

the interviewers: If you've been doing a lot of talking, right. That's true — if you end up talking all the time, like in a session yesterday where you talked a lot during the debrief, you may even have that kind of thing. If you just talk a lot during a day, you can have it.

title: NASA-UAP-D026, Apollo 14 Debriefing, 1971
text:
the crew: I don't have too much else to do in here, Charles.

the interviewers: Yeah, I know. We're looking for somebody to cut a glove. Who is it? When is that going to happen, Bill?

the crew: A comment on the Afrin bottles: the pressure gets to them and they separate into a jillion bubbles. That emulsion is very bubbly and filled with air. As soon as you take the cap off, it comes out and starts leaking. Yeah, and it's kind of difficult to control that stuff when you use it.

the interviewers: Was that the first time you opened the bottle, or after?

the crew: Always. Every time you open it.

the interviewers: Okay, thanks. What technique did you use for applying the nose drops? How did you put them in?

the crew: Very gentle squeeze, trying to get just one drop at a time out — just put the dropper up and let her go. Put it in there and hosed it.

the interviewers: Just like we told him. Okay, good boy. Did you tape those PRDs down in your suits?

the crew: Tape them? You'll never believe it, Charles — we had zipper pockets.

title: NASA-UAP-D026, Apollo 14 Debriefing, 1971
text:
the interviewers: You're kidding!

the crew: No, it's unbelievable. We pulled out those coveralls and there were zippers on them. First time we've seen zippers in an old committee type [sic].

the interviewers: So they're not on the training suits, just on the flight suits, is that it?

the crew: Apparently we had requested them way, way back and forgotten that we'd made the official request. It was already in the mail and nobody knew about it. None of the training devices were that way, but lo and behold, out of the package they came, and there were the Zippy Sticks [sic]. They were nice.

the interviewers: Well, that's great. The question on the checklist, Chuck, is whether to remind them to put them back into the coveralls — you want to know if we should put it on the checklist.

the crew: Okay. Well, I don't understand what that is.

the interviewers: When you remove your PGAs, is there a point in the checklist where we should include removing the PRDs back into your flight coveralls, or is that not there?

the crew: It already says take all the items out of there.

the interviewers: Oh, it does? Okay. Well, it's listed in there when we take the suits off that first day. And then when you bring the suits back over from the LM — pretty rushed timeline — I don't know if it would be any good to put that in your timeline book, because at that time your main purpose is just to get the suits stowed. You said you jerked them down and got them zipped up in those bags pretty fast.

the crew: Right into the bag. Probably wouldn't hurt — when we list the items to take out of the suits when we come back to the LM, we can just add PRDs in there as another item. We list sunglasses and pencils and all the rest.

the interviewers: Sunglasses reminds me. When you said you used sunglasses — you were the only one who used them. Corrective lenses, is that right?

the crew: I used prescription lenses.

title: NASA-UAP-D026, Apollo 14 Debriefing, 1971
text:
the interviewers: When did you use the corrective lenses?

the crew: A couple of times when I had to read small print in the flight plan. Just in the command module — with the helmet off. I didn't use them in the helmet.

the interviewers: No, I didn't think you did.

the crew: I'd use them from time to time in the simulators, particularly in the LMS. The only time I can't adapt is in low light.

the interviewers: Did you have any feeling about that on the lunar surface — that the light levels were bothersome to you because of that? Because that is a very typical thing.

the crew: That's an interesting point. No, the light levels were generally higher in the lunar module. The thing you don't simulate on the LMS is the difference between day and night on the side of the moon — the LMS is dark all the time, for all practical purposes.

the interviewers: How about out on the surface, when you were actually out there with your visor down? Did those light levels bother you at all? Did you feel you were having any difficulties?

the crew: The only problem I have is reading small print at close distances when the light level is low. I had that problem a couple of times in the CMS and the LMS — I don't know how many times I broke them out, perhaps 6 or 8 times.

the interviewers: To read that deck card — it's about the only time I've ever seen you use them.

the crew: But on the surface, Chuck, it's either stark white — dazzling white — or it's absolutely black. So I don't think eyesight has a great deal to do with it at that point.

the interviewers: That's right. I think you've covered the vision on the surface pretty well in here — you've done that very well. I don't think we need to go further; if something comes back up, we'll give you the word. But as far as I can tell, I think we've got most of that covered.

the crew: I might point out, if you want to pursue the visibility further for any sort of medical thing: if you look at the photographs, in my opinion they're exactly what we saw.

title: NASA-UAP-D026, Apollo 14 Debriefing, 1971
text:
the interviewers: Is that right?

the crew: If you look cross-sun, the visibility is great. If you look up-sun, everything's glared out by the sun. If you look down-sun, all of the gentle, subtle rolling and subdued craters just disappear on you. But cross-sun visibility is great — the photographs show it the same way. Just real briefly on that same subject — it's kind of hard to tell when you're looking at just negatives of these 70mm, but I was looking at some of the zero-phase pictures last night, and the targets would disappear at zero phase; it does it on the films also. I'll have to see what the prints look like, but my first impression is that I didn't see much more than what the camera did at zero phase — which surprises me, because I would have thought different. But I don't take that as any sort of data until I've had a chance to see a blown-up print; I'm just looking at some negatives in here. That's my first impression.

the interviewers: We've always said that the eyeball can see more than the film can, but with our particular film I think there's pretty good correspondence.

the crew: You're not insinuating that we have bad eyeballs, are you?

the interviewers: No, we just have good film. That's a preliminary opinion.

the crew: On the sunglasses — as far as I know, nobody even broke their sunglasses out.

the interviewers: And you didn't feel you needed them?

the crew: No. Well, the only time we needed them was when there was sun shafting in, but in PTC, if you just wait a couple of minutes, it'll be gone.

the interviewers: There was a time at 196 hours where we lost your respiration, or your CPN [sic]. Did you notice — was the signal conditioner disconnected then, or was there a sensor loose or anything?

the crew: No, there was nothing different. It just quit, apparently.

the interviewers: You couldn't see anything obvious as to why?

title: NASA-UAP-D026, Apollo 14 Debriefing, 1971
text:
the crew: No, I went over the whole system — we checked the sensors, checked the belt, checked the connection. We were getting too close to entry to really do a great deal of troubleshooting, so there was no point.

the interviewers: Okay, fine, but we're going to check those things. We never had a signal conditioner as such fail, and that's one of the things that's sort of interesting — it wasn't a sensor problem. We want to be sure and check those signal conditioners now. Okay, I think we've got most of this mobility thing done.

the crew: I was talking about that biomed belt. Let me just say that I think my urine bag problem — the UCTA problem — is kind of related to that belt, in that the UCTA is held by that elastic strap. And I think the problem in getting the hose length correct has to do with the fact that the UCTA doesn't always end up in the same place. You try to get it below the belt so it doesn't get on top and increase the dimension any more than you've already done. And I think in doing that, I probably wore the gun down on the hip more. In retrospect, if there were some way that thing could be fixed just like the biomed belt is fixed, then it wouldn't move up and down, and you could adjust the hose length a little better. I wore mine differently — I wore mine over the biomed belt. That may be the difference. And fixing the vertical height of that thing, so you can't get the right movement — because mine was up and down. I think when you reached in, you probably thought it was sagging down as a result of being full of fluid on one hand, but also because I used to wear it below the belt on the other. But his hose had a definite kink in it — it came out of the fitting and just made a sharp kink, bent just like you see the hose.

the interviewers: Did you feel any real dryness of skin, or dryness of your lips or your nose at all? Did you ever have any sensation that way?

the crew: Not exceptionally, for me. I sure didn't have any obvious sensation of dryness. I don't know if he did — I noticed his lips were cracking about the 4th or 5th day after we got back from TEI, but I don't know if you got it or not. No, I didn't feel dry. In fact, I noticed the cracking in here too. But no, I didn't feel any dryness particularly.

the interviewers: Okay, I think we've got these all covered. Did they talk to you about the— Phil Chapman wanted to tack on the light flash thing on the end of this here. So once you tell him to come on in, let him get that out of the way. Hey, just real fast, I know you've got to take the data and you're looking ahead to the longer flights.

title: NASA-UAP-D026, Apollo 14 Debriefing, 1971
text:
the crew: 5 pounds is no— it just comes and goes with no problem at all. Is it really a total body water loss?

the interviewers: That'll be a real important plug to hang on there. That's why we'll go over that with you so that it is clear.

the crew: We won't have total body water or extracellular fluid space until after quarantine. That will be done at Baylor. Those are beta meters. We're just doing the gamma counting in here.

the interviewers: Oh, we'll argue that with you later. Let's get it out. I'll talk with you later about it.

the crew: There's a sign that says go. Bill, go ask him. They suggested that we should tack on a few questions about light flashes.

the interviewers: Deke suggested that we should tack on a few questions about light flashes to the end of this briefing. That's what we're about to do. What we'd like to do is to clarify some of the subjective impressions that you got of what you saw in the way of light flashes, and also to clarify the conditions under which you saw them. Excuse me, could you stand back from the mic just a little bit? That's a boom mic. Larry, you need to get reasonably close to the mic. Is there a way that this room could be darkened? Okay, first question we got is, the streaks that you saw, were they a very sharp phenomenon or were they rather diffuse?

the crew: The ones I saw were very sharp. There was no mistaking what it was. It was a streak so long, instantaneously disappeared. Yeah, I think that's correct. Both the single streak and the double shot appeared to be very clear to me.

the interviewers: They were quite clear, and I think I made the comment over the loop.

title: NASA-UAP-D026, Apollo 14 Debriefing, 1971
text:
the crew: Most of my streaks appeared to be on the periphery. And for the first several days, I got the impression that this direction was predominant. Later on, it appeared I don't think I could get that good a pattern, but that was my first impression for the first couple of days.

the interviewers: The next question is, was there any apparent direction of propagation? Could you tell it was coming from one side to the other, or was it just flat?

the crew: Several times you did say from the left to the right or something like that. Tried to correlate it, but in my case I couldn't really correlate a pattern on it. Yeah, I would think that the time period in which we tried to report them streak by streak, flash by flash, was representative. And it was my feeling that it was generally random during that time period, and therefore generally random throughout the time that we were noticing them.

the interviewers: No, I meant, could you detect that it was moving from one side to the other in general? It was moving in a particular direction, but you could see it as a travel from one side to the other. You really could.

the crew: Yes, you can see it as a travel on one side. I think we tried to report it that way, didn't we? That's the way it was coming, because it has to be very fast, you know.

the interviewers: Yes, you did report it. That's the way it was puzzling us, because it has to be very fast, you know. Was there some character to these flashes that had some aspect of direction? I mean, were they all the same rod-shaped, or did they have a tail on them?

the crew: Well, what I saw, what I reported as a streak, was simply that. Now, maybe the way we determined the direction subconsciously was that it was a ball of light moving in a direction, leaving a tail. But I don't— I can't say that for sure. All I reported was a streak, and I had the impression of it moving from one direction to the other. And I reported that direction, and I can't clarify it much more than that.

the interviewers: Maybe while you're asking a question, if we just douse the lights. I think they can see this in the darkened room, but just try it. The idea is to try to see whether this is what you saw or similar to it.

title: NASA-UAP-D026, Apollo 14 Debriefing, 1971
text:
the interviewers: Well, can you see anything?

the crew: Yeah, except that's what it looked like, except it was traveling. In other words, it started out and it definitely progressed across the field of view.

the interviewers: You saw it as a point and it made a streak.

the crew: I never did see 2 simultaneously either.

the interviewers: Neither did I. You have 2 streaks, right? I never saw that.

the crew: At one time you said you saw a semicolon-shaped thing. Saw what? A semicolon.
